speakers: Mark (guest, quantitative macro researcher and professor)
Alan Dunne (guest host, Top Traders Unplugged)
summary: Top Traders Unplugged Ep.388 (Feb 2026): peak-bubble in metals and softs, rotation out of the US, and the fiscal versus monetary dominance regime with a possible new Fed chair. Mark stresses that asset relationships are regime-conditional, urges regime and change-point detection and causal modelling over factor-zoo overfitting, and still backs trend following.

coverage.note: peak bubble in metals and softs, bubble ingredients, retail habitat
gold ETF flows and central bank buying, AI narrative shift
EM vs US inflation, K-shaped economy, uncertainty premium
safe asset relative, bonds diversify, regimes give an edge
conditional relationships, beta regimes, dollar and gold
hidden Markov, VIX thresholds, regime types, stock-bond correlation and alternatives
fiscal dominance definition, WWII, war-like debt
pandemic fiscal excess, financial repression, Treasury incentives
economy hot, balance sheet, Treasury auctions
bubble risk from low rates, fiscal theory of price level
robustness, trend following persistence; outro and sponsor read

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the sock gen CTA index up 1.1% um and the sock gen trend index slightly better at 1.15%
claims.claim: February 2026 to date: SG CTA +1.1%, SG Trend +1.15%, both +5.9% YTD, led by gold higher, cocoa and coffee trending down, energy and US bonds rising, currencies choppy.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we had this the spike in gold and we and silver. We've had a little bit of reversal.
claims.claim: Mark thinks metals (and softs such as cocoa 12 to 4, coffee) may have peaked as bubbles after January 2026.
claims.testable: partly - bubble top calls are hard to test

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: you could have a a blowoff top that you might have some correction and then sometimes that they'll just slowly you know just you know uh grind lower
claims.claim: Bubbles end with a blow-off top then correction, sometimes a slow grind lower, so trend followers can profit on both sides if they exit near the top.
claims.direction: long into the bubble, short after the top
claims.testable: yes - trend-following P&L around bubble tops

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: you're going to need sort of the fuel which is excess money which I think we still have but you also need a narrative and a story associated with a bubble
claims.claim: Bubbles need excess money and a narrative, and narratives form around assets that are hard to value.
claims.testable: partly - proxies for liquidity and valuation difficulty

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: they actually gravitate to hardto value stocks.
claims.claim: Retail investors gravitate to hard-to-value stocks (retail habitat), so optimistic narratives push such stocks to extremes (tech).

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: So if you have some optimistic euphoria whether it be in silver or gold where are you going to get the supply is the supply is constrained so you could have these demand shocks
claims.claim: Commodity bubbles differ from equity bubbles because mining supply is constrained, so demand shocks translate into price spikes.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: ETF flow was was very much the dominant driver in the latter part of the year
claims.claim: In 2025 central-bank gold buying fell and ETF (retail) flows dominated, consistent with retail-driven momentum.
claims.indicator: gold ETF flows, World Gold Council central bank buying

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: those countries that feel as though that there might be a potential risk of sanctions have been bigger buyers their central banks have been bigger buyers than other central banks
claims.claim: Central banks of countries fearing US sanctions (China, Poland, former Soviet states) buy more gold as a quasi safe asset outside the dollar.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: I think that narrative is is a is the use of storytelling when we don't have what
claims.claim: Narrative is the use of storytelling when risk is not countable; the AI story shifted from all positive to winners and losers.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: a risk is something that's measurable. I can count it.
claims.claim: Risk is countable (volatility, VIX) while uncertainty is not, because there are no past events to count.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: since I this is new technology I don't have a way to actually measure the countable uh risk.
claims.claim: AI is new technology with uncountable uncertainty, so valuations rest on narrative and the growth embedded in prices can be too high or too low.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: rotation is probably the major theme for 2026
claims.claim: 2026 theme is rotation: out of the US into Europe and global stocks, flows from US pensions abroad, software down and real assets up, and US bond buyers hedging currency.
claims.indicator: US vs ex-US equity flows, hedged US bond buying

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: more you know uh buying across the diverse set of companies than what we saw in 2025
claims.claim: Equity market breadth broadened in early 2026 versus concentrated 2025.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: if you look at a you know basket of em countries and then you look at their inflation, it's actually lower than US inflation even now.
claims.claim: EM inflation is below US core inflation (about 3%), making EM more attractive and driving rotation toward EM, along with higher EM real yields.
claims.indicator: EM inflation vs US inflation, real yields

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we have this K-shaped economy uh where we have very difference between the real economy and then the asset economy in the US
claims.claim: A K-shaped US economy, where real economy and asset economy diverge, shapes asset flows worldwide.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: if there's more uncertainty, you'd say like, well, I'm going to need a premium to hold a risky asset in a high uncertain country versus a less uncertain country.
claims.claim: Higher US trade/geopolitical/monetary uncertainty demands a premium, pushing flows to less uncertain countries and weakening US assets as safe assets.
claims.indicator: trade, geopolitical and monetary uncertainty indices

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: you could still be a safe asset the US treasury but it might be less safe than it was a year ago or two years ago
claims.claim: Safety is relative: treasuries remain safe but less so, so investors diversify more of their flows.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the Fed cuts rate aggressively and bonds rally while equities go down and bonds do diversify
claims.claim: Bonds are a less reliable but not a failed equity diversifier; in crises with aggressive Fed cuts they still diversify.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: by being aware of we'll call it the you know regime changes or how all of our analysis is conditional then you might be able to get an edge
claims.claim: Awareness of regimes, in which relationships change, gives an edge in portfolio formation.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: of our asset price relationships are conditional on the environment we live in
claims.claim: Asset price relationships are conditional on environment, e.g. stock beta is not a single number.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: the concept of a beta for a uh individual stock is a fairly fluid one
claims.claim: A stock's beta differs across crisis/non-crisis and recession/non-recession regimes.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: prior to liberation day, the dollar was kind of strong on on talk of tariffs
claims.claim: The dollar-rate differential relationship weakened after Liberation Day (a credibility discount), and gold has risen independent of real yields and the dollar.
claims.indicator: USD vs rate differentials, gold vs real yields

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: if we're in a higher risk regime or higher risk environment that that the behavior different uh strategies and tactics are different than if you're in a low volatility regime
claims.claim: Strategy behaviour differs by volatility regime, which can be identified with hidden Markov models.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: once it gets above like 25 and it's and it's moving higher. So it's above a certain threshold level and moving higher is that it's bad news for a lot of assets.
claims.claim: VIX above about 25 and rising is bad for many assets; around 40 is a peak, a signal to re-enter.
claims.direction: reduce risk above 25 and rising; re-enter near 40

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: then we know it's sort of peaking and then we know it's going to come back the other way and that's good news to get back in
claims.claim: A VIX near 40 marks a peak and a buy-back-in point.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: inflation goes up that usually then that that that stock uh bond correlation is also going to go higher
claims.claim: Stock-bond correlation is inflation-dependent, so third factors indicate the regime.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: But when that correlation starts to go positive and rates are lower, they say like, well, that's a great time to own a lot of hedge fund strategies
claims.claim: When stock-bond correlation turns positive and rates are lower, hold more alternatives; when strongly negative with high rates, alternatives are less needed.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: knowing the regime that we're in could help us you know on the margin change our our our tilts and our exposures
claims.claim: Regime knowledge adjusts trend-based portfolio tilts to avoid overexposure to one sector.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: fiscal dominance says that debt is so high that central bank or we're going to put pressure on the central bank to use its powers to control interest rates and then buy up excess debt
claims.claim: Fiscal dominance, when debt forces monetary policy to hold rates down and buy debt, is a risk but not yet reached; WWII shows the precedent.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: there's usually inflation because of perhaps pent-up demand after the war ends is that you don't want to be a debt holder
claims.claim: Debt is not safe in war or war-like episodes since inflation follows, and the pandemic had the same features.
claims.direction: avoid bonds after war-like fiscal expansion

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: that's why we had a sort of inflation burst because of the excesses of fiscal policy
claims.claim: The post-pandemic inflation burst came from excess fiscal policy that was never reversed, creating a fiscal-monetary tussle.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you you you pin down long-term rates and you allow inflation to be higher. So bond holders experience negative returns
claims.claim: Financial repression in the 1940s pinned long rates while allowing inflation, giving bondholders negative real returns until the Fed regained independence.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: what's the easiest way to reduce the value of your nominal debt is that if you have inflation
claims.claim: The Treasury wants lower rates and tolerates higher inflation to lower the real value of debt.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: I may want to run an economy hotter because I don't believe the data that I have
claims.claim: Employment benchmark revisions (about 1 million fewer jobs) give an administration reason to run the economy hotter.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: he's going to reduce the amount of uh of of treasuries on the Fed balance sheet that's reducing overall liquidity that's going to cause a major deleveraging
claims.claim: If the new Fed chair (Warsh) shrinks the balance sheet, liquidity falls and asset markets deleverage, which the Treasury does not want.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we did like a uh $700 billion of treasuries being auctioned in one week
claims.claim: About $700bn of Treasuries was auctioned in one week, so absorption depends on demand staying firm.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it would run the economy hot and potentially fuel acid bubbles as well
claims.claim: Lower rates because of debt concerns would run the economy hot and fuel asset bubbles.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: people are going to take your money out of uh uh you know going to start to buy real assets as opposed to you know uh debt assets if there's the expectation of permanent large deficits
claims.claim: Cochrane's fiscal theory of the price level: expected permanent deficits drive money into real assets and inflation, as seen in gold, with financial assets bid up if savings are abundant.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: he follows through on what he says he's going to do, we're going to be in a very different monetary regime
claims.claim: The Fed chair outcome could change the monetary regime: smaller balance sheet, fiscal dominance, or continued deficits; uncertainty is high.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: be prepared for something that may be different than what you're reading about in the newspapers
claims.claim: Appointed officials often behave differently than expected, so prepare for uncertainty.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: we have technology to uh to what we call change point detection to sort of see if there's a change or break in a in a in in a time series
claims.claim: Change-point detection and hidden Markov models detect breaks, though only after the break; macro awareness improves sensitivity.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: We think of it as a network.
claims.claim: Model markets as a network of causal connections and watch how connections change through time to get ahead of regime shifts.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: the number one issue in finance now
claims.claim: Identifying causality is the main issue in finance, with AI causal-discovery challenges.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: you find them in the training set or we find them in past history then we look at them in the future and they no longer exist
claims.claim: The factor zoo: factors found in past data often vanish out of sample, so seek causal factors and check models against data.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: it's not the complexity of the technique that matters. it's the number of features that we have or it's the domain knowledge we have that actually adds more value
claims.claim: Research shows features and domain knowledge add more than model complexity in machine learning.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: machine learning is very good on stationary data
claims.claim: Machine learning works on stationary data but struggles on non-stationary adaptive markets (Lo).

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: your benchmark standard should be more simpler models
claims.claim: Use simple models as benchmark; learn AI but do not over-optimise.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: I still believe in in trend following it still seems to say that it works especially in uncertain regimes especially when data is non-stationary
claims.claim: Trend following works especially in uncertain regimes and non-stationary data, but crowding makes improvement hard.

claims.speaker: Mark
claims.quote: There are periods uh that when it does really well then my period where where it it waines in performance and it goes back
claims.claim: Trend following and momentum alternate strong and weak periods; Mark is confident over five years but not over five months.
